quests.passageTopic: Opinion: What a Library Is For
quests.passage: Whenever a council needs to cut spending, someone suggests that libraries are a relic. Books, the argument goes, are now cheaper than ever and available online. This view mistakes the library's product for its purpose. Consider who uses the Hillfield branch on a weekday morning: job seekers using the free computers to complete applications, new arrivals attending English conversation groups, parents with toddlers at story time, and older residents who come, quite simply, for company. Few of them are there for a book they could not otherwise afford. The branch is, in effect, one of the last public spaces where nobody is required to buy anything, and where staff will help with a form, a printer, or a problem. A council that measures its libraries only by the number of loans is measuring the wrong thing, much as one might judge a school by how many pencils it uses. Cuts made on that basis will save money that is later spent elsewhere, on services that struggle to reach the same people.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Do Later School Start Times Help?
quests.passageTopic: Do Later School Start Times Help?
quests.passage: Several districts have moved their high school start times from 7:30 to 8:30 a.m., hoping that teenagers, whose body clocks shift later during adolescence, would sleep more and learn better. The early results are encouraging but uneven. In one district, students reported sleeping an extra 45 minutes on school nights, and first-period attendance rose by 8 percent. Another district found no change in test scores after two years, though students reported feeling less tired. Researchers note a difficulty: when school starts later, it also ends later, which can push back sports practice and part-time work, and some students simply stay up later to compensate. Parents with early work hours also face new problems, since they can no longer drop children off on their way to the office. The evidence suggests that later starts help most when they are combined with consistent bedtimes and adjusted afternoon schedules, rather than adopted on their own.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: The Last Game
quests.passage: Old Mr. Petrov had played chess in the park every Sunday for as long as anyone could remember, and the young man who sat opposite him that afternoon had clearly been warned. He moved his pieces quickly, with the confidence of someone who had beaten most of the people he had ever played. Mr. Petrov said little. He lost a pawn, then a knight, and the young man began to smile. Around the board, the regulars who had gathered were strangely quiet, and a few of them were looking at their shoes. On the thirty-first move, Mr. Petrov slid a bishop across the board with two fingers, almost carelessly, and said, "I believe that is mate in three." The young man stared. He examined the board for a long minute, and when he looked up his smile was gone. "You let me take the knight," he said. Mr. Petrov shrugged. "It seemed generous."

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Why Translations of Poems Differ
quests.passage: Ask five translators to render the same short poem, and you will receive five poems. This is not because some of them are careless. A poem is not only what it says but how it says it: the rhythm, the sounds, the associations of particular words. Translators must decide which of these to keep, because they cannot keep all of them. One may choose to preserve the literal meaning, producing a version accurate but flat. Another may aim to preserve the music, adjusting the words to keep the rhythm, at the cost of precision. A third may try to recreate the effect on the reader, which can mean changing an image to one that carries the same feeling in the new language. None of these approaches is simply wrong. Readers who want to understand a poem should, if possible, read two or three translations side by side, since the differences between them reveal what the original contains.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: The Summer the Thames Smelled
quests.passage: In the summer of 1858, London's river became unbearable. For years the city had been pouring sewage into the Thames, and an unusually hot, dry season turned the water into a slow-moving mass of waste. The smell was so strong that Parliament, which sits beside the river, hung curtains soaked in chemicals at its windows and considered moving elsewhere. Doctors had long argued that disease was spread by foul air, so the smell frightened politicians in a way that arguments about water quality had not. Within weeks, a bill authorizing a new system of sewers passed with unusual speed. The engineer Joseph Bazalgette built a network that carried waste downstream and away from the center, and the cholera outbreaks that had killed thousands in earlier decades stopped. Ironically, the theory that persuaded politicians to act, that bad air carried disease, was wrong; the real danger had been the contaminated water. Yet the reform worked anyway.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Two Ways to Run a Meeting
quests.passageTopic: Two Ways to Run a Meeting
quests.passage: At Marlow Design, weekly meetings once ran for ninety minutes, with each person reporting on their projects in turn. Attendance was high, and so was irritation. Last year the director replaced them with a different format: a one-page summary is circulated the evening before, the meeting lasts thirty minutes, and it is spent only on decisions and disagreements. Supporters say the change saves each employee about an hour a week and forces people to prepare. A staff survey after six months showed opinion divided almost evenly. Critics point out that the new meeting is less social; the old format, however tedious, kept people informed about each other's work and gave quieter colleagues a chance to speak. The director concedes the loss and has introduced a monthly lunch, on the grounds that it is better to be honest about the purpose of a gathering than to disguise a social need as a status update.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: An Ordinary Kindness
quests.passage: The bus was late, the rain was heavy, and I had just received an email that made my week harder. When I finally boarded, I took the last free seat, folded my wet umbrella onto my lap, and stared at nothing. At the next stop, an elderly man climbed on, looked around, and began to make his way toward the back, gripping the handrails. I considered standing. I did not. I was tired, I told myself, and he looked more capable than he moved. A teenage girl across the aisle got up without a word and gestured to her seat. He thanked her warmly. "It's nothing," she said, and went back to her phone. I have not forgotten the moment. Nothing happened to me; I did nothing wrong, exactly. But I keep returning to how easily I had arranged my reasons, and how little they weighed against her quiet standing.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: School Cafeteria Audit: Food Waste
quests.passage: An audit of five school cafeterias found that students throw away an average of 28 percent of the food they are served. Fruit and vegetables account for the largest share by weight, and waste is highest in the meal served immediately before recess, when students are eager to leave. Cafeterias that moved recess to before lunch saw waste fall by about a third. Students interviewed said they prefer to eat after playing, because they feel hungrier. The report suggests that this single scheduling change does more than redesigning menus, although healthier menus are worth pursuing on other grounds. It cautions against drawing broad conclusions: three of the five schools shared a district, and one school changed its supplier during the audit, which may have affected the results. The authors recommend a larger study before any district-wide changes are made, but note that moving recess costs almost nothing and can be tested immediately.

quests.passage: Dear Ms. Alder, Please accept this letter as formal notice of my resignation from the post of operations coordinator, effective 30 November. I have valued my four years with the company and the colleagues with whom I have worked, many of whom I count as friends. Over the past year, my role has expanded considerably, and while my responsibilities have grown, my title and salary have not. I raised this on two occasions and was told that the matter would be reviewed. I understand that budgets are limited, and I do not write this to apportion blame. I mention it only because I would not want my successor to be told the same. I will do everything I can to ensure a smooth handover before I leave.
